title: Engineering Audience Playbook - Tactical Messaging and Competitive Notes
content:
Purpose / one-liner: Quick-reference playbook for SDRs, solutions engineers, and content writers to tailor messaging to three decision-making personas: ML engineers, backend engineers, and platform teams. Focus: reduce time-to-proof, emphasize predictable economics + operational controls, and call out competitive differentiators vs public cloud managed endpoints and open-source self-hosted runtimes.

Audience framing (short):
- ML engineers: prioritize fidelity, model interchangeability, experiment velocity, reproducible evals. Care about prompt-conditional quality, eval tooling, and guardrails for drift.
- Backend engineers: prioritize latency, predictable p99s/p95s, simple SDKs/integration, and low operational overhead. Care about retries/fallbacks, quotas, and cost per request.
- Platform teams: prioritize governance, multi-tenant cost accounting, rollout controls, private deployments (VPC/HSM), and SLAs. Care about observability, policy controls, and migration paths.

Core value props to highlight by persona:
- ML engineers: "Swap models fast, test reliably, and keep costs from wrecking experiments." Emphasize model catalog, eval hooks, per-prompt quality monitoring, and deterministic version pinning. Call out Redwood Optimize suggestions for quantization & batching that preserve quality.
- Backend engineers: "Predictable latency and lower per-token spend with minimal changes to your existing stack." Emphasize runtime batching, KV/prefix caching, streaming responses, HTTP/SDK parity, and fallback policies.
- Platform teams: "Unified control plane across hosted, dedicated, private with auditability and billing granularity." Emphasize token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, canary/A-B rollouts, and KMS/HSM integration.

30s elevator scripts (use depending on persona):
- ML engineer: "If you need to iterate on models quickly without re-architecting infra, Redwood gives you a model catalog, eval hooks, and safe rollouts so you can test new checkpoints and measure regressions before they hit users."
- Backend engineer: "Redwood is an inference runtime that matches familiar HTTP SDKs and delivers predictable p99 latency via batching, cache, and optimized kernels — so you can run LLMs like any other service without token bill shock."
- Platform lead: "Redwood unifies hosted, reserved, and private inference under one control plane with SLAs, audit logs, and cost attribution, so you can standardize ML serving without building ops plumbing yourself."

2-minute pitch + technical bullets (for SEs):
- Start: 1) Problem: ad-hoc LLM serving leads to spiky costs, latency variance, and slow experiments. 2) Redwood approach: runtime + orchestration + routing + Optimize.
- Technical bullets by persona:
  - ML engineers: model version pinning, eval regression alerts, per-prompt metrics, A/B evals, dataset-driven quality monitoring, and integration with existing model training pipelines.
  - Backend engineers: continuous batching, KV/prefix cache, streaming token-by-token output, autoscale policies for reserved pools, and graceful fallback to cheaper variants under load.
  - Platform teams: per-customer routing policies, private control plane option (VPC + on-prem), KMS/HSM key management, RBAC + SAML, and long retention audit logs.

Objection handling (short list):
- "We already use cloud managed endpoints": emphasize predictable unit economics, built-in batching/caching (reduces per-token cost), contiguous control over fallbacks, and model-variant routing that avoids hard downtimes.
- "We self-host open-source runtimes": emphasize ops cost/time-to-value — Redwood provides an optimized kernel/serving runtime and a control plane; for Private deployments we enable air-gapped or VPC installs so you keep control without reinventing autoscaling, rollouts, and billing.
- "We care about model quality not cost": we pair Optimize's quantization and batching suggestions with per-prompt quality monitoring and regression alerts so you can find the cost/quality sweet spot and detect degradation early.

Competitive cues and short rebuttals: (use when sales rep names competitors)
- Public cloud AI endpoints (BigCloud AIA, ComputeCloud LLM): "Cloud endpoint gives model access but not predictable unit economics at scale; Redwood controls batching, cache, and routing to reduce token spend and provides dedicated reserves for throughput-sensitive workloads."
- Inference vendors (SelfHostRuntimes, FastServe): "Those give runtime but often lack the rollout/tracing/quality tooling and enterprise control plane Redwood offers — we combine runtime performance with observability and rollout mechanics."
- Open-source runtime + in-house orchestration: "Building and maintaining autoscaling, quantization compatibility, regression monitoring, and a unified billing/tenant model is expensive and distracts from product work. Redwood's private option offloads that while preserving network/security constraints."

Persona-specific tactical talk-tracks (copyable snippets):
- ML engineer Slack/Email opener: "Hi — curious whether you’ve had model rollouts get noisy in prod. We have an eval-based rollout flow and regression alerts that catch prompt-level drops before they hit users. Can I share a short notebook to demo?"
- Backend engineer Slack/Email opener: "Quick question — do your p95/p99s for LLM calls vary after traffic spikes? We have a batching + autoscale reserve model that keeps p99s tight while lowering per-token cost; can we run a 2-week perf comparison?"
- Platform lead Slack/Email opener: "Want to compare tenant-level cost attribution and SLA tooling? We can map your current endpoints to a pilot flow (hosted or VPC) and show cost/latency tradeoffs for key routes."

Suggested two-week POC skeletons (so SEs can propose fast):
- ML engineer POC: 1) 2 weeks, 1-2 devs, 1 model family; integrate SDK, ingest 500-1000 eval prompts, run A/B between current model and Redwood-hosted variant; enable eval alerts. Success metrics: no material quality regression, <12h iteration cycle for model swap, reproducible eval reports.
- Backend engineer POC: 1) 2 weeks, simple proxy route; measure p95/p99 delta, token cost per 10k requests, and observe streaming latency. Success metrics: p99 improvement or parity with lower cost, stable throughput at target qps.
- Platform POC: 2 weeks, map 2 routes across tenants, enable per-route dashboards and rollout policy. Success metrics: cost attribution per tenant, canary rollout executed, audit logs available for review.

Messaging experiments (A/B ideas + metrics):
- Subject lines to test for emails to engineers: A) "Cut per-token spend without sacrificing quality" vs B) "Tighten p99 latency for LLM calls". Metrics: open rate, reply rate, demo booked.
- SE demo hooks: A) focus on a live p99 demo vs B) focus on an eval/regression demo. Metrics: conversion to POC, POC-to-purchase in 90 days.

Collateral checklist for content team:
- Short notebook showing eval-based rollback.
- Lightweight perf benchmark comparing p95/p99 across 3 model sizes on CPU/GPU.
- One-pager: "When to choose Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private" targeted to platform leads.
- Demo script for SEs: live swap of model checkpoint + show regression alert firing.

Open questions / places to iterate (notes to self):
- Do we have a canonical latency/cost micro-benchmark that’s neutral (no model favoritism) to share in POCs? If not, build one Q1.
- Need clear checklist for security questionnaire items for private installs (bring into security-and-compliance docs).
- Draft Slack snippets for SDR sequences that call out specific GitHub/Jira integrations (make them concrete).

Quick handoff checklist for SE before kickoff:
1) Confirm persona & primary metric (quality vs latency vs governance).
2) Select model family + baseline prompts.
3) Share access to telemetry (or replicate sample traffic for SE to run against).
4) Pre-configure rollout policy and a canary route.
5) Define POC success metrics and who signs off.

Notes / research pointers:
- Pull performance kernels doc from infra (link in linked_artifacts).
- Ask applied-ml for recommended eval prompts (Zhang Wei).
- Talk to SRE about reserved pool sizing recommended defaults for p99 targets.

End of doc. Keep this short-form playbook available for SEs and GTM writers; iterate based on POC feedback.
